The curriculum covers large language models (LLMs), autonomous AI agents, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), multi-agent orchestration and production deployment. The programme also covers RAG, which allows AI applications to retrieve information from external documents and databases when generating responses. Practical exercises will take participants from building individual assistants to developing systems that coordinate multiple agents. highlights.content: * share this! * [Share](#) --- October 30, 2026 # Engineering researcher seeks to prevent AI agents from going rogue by Harrem Monkhorst, [University of Florida](http://www.ufl.edu/) edited by [Swati Mestri](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-team/), reviewed by [Andrew Zinin](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-team/) ![](https://scx1.b-cdn.net/gfx/profiles/a5155b7e93ee6855.png) ##### Swati Mestri Scientific Editor Meet our [editorial team](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-team/) Behind our [editorial process](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-process/) ![](https://scx1.b-cdn.net/gfx/profiles/2fa26e993b2d1988.png) ##### Andrew Zinin Chief Editor Meet our [editorial team](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-team/) Behind our [editorial process](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-process/) [Editors' notes](javascript:void(0)) This article has been reviewed according to Science X's [editorial process](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-process/) and [policies](https://sciencex.com/help/editorial-standards/). University of Florida computer science professor Sumit Jha, Ph.D., is working to keep agents from "going rogue." Jha and his team have developed a system that can detect when an AI model begins to drift from its assigned task and steer it back without retraining the model or adding significant computing demands. The research comes as news reports have chronicled [AI agents](https://techxplore.com/news/2025-01-ai-agents-taxes-holidays.html?utm_source=embeddings&utm_medium=related&utm_campaign=internal) gaining more autonomy and occasionally behaving in ways their developers did not intend. Recent incidents have included AI agents accessing government websites and an Anthropic model submitting an anonymous tip to a police department in July, claiming to have information about an unsolved murder. Jha, a professor in UF's Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering, or CISE, studies how to make AI systems more controllable and understandable. He is working to engineer simple, noninvasive tweaks to keep systems on task. ## Correcting drift inside the model Jha and his collaborators have authored a paper titled "Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-agent AI," detailing a system dubbed ATLAS, which stands for Algebraic Task–role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory. The acronym hints at the dense mathematics at the heart of the system. Jha and his co-authors, Vishal Pramanik, Maisha Maliha and Susmit Jha, devised a system that works inside the large language model, or LLM, as it generates output. When the model begins to drift from its task, the ATLAS system steers the LLM back toward the assignment, as well as its original responsibility and the latest shared information. The paper has been accepted for the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, or [EMNLP](https://2026.emnlp.org/), Oct. 24–29 in Budapest. "An AI agent can start going wrong before its response looks wrong," Jha explained. "Inside the model, it may already be drifting from the task, confusing its role or relying on information that has been replaced. ATLAS is built to correct that drift before it reaches the next message, so other agents do not build on the mistake." Edited by Barnabas Oretan (The Tech Buzz).AI-generated image [Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=techbuzz.ai) [Nvidia](https://www.nvidia.com) is weighing an unprecedented move to cosign financing for Nscale's AI data center project in West Virginia, marking a dramatic shift in how chipmakers are supporting infrastructure buildout. The potential arrangement comes as investors grow increasingly nervous about the sustainability of AI spending, threatening to choke off capital for the very data centers that house Nvidia's chips. It's a striking reversal - the company that sparked the AI gold rush now finds itself potentially backstopping the picks-and-shovels builders. [Nvidia](https://www.nvidia.com) is exploring a financing arrangement that would have been unthinkable just months ago - acting as a cosigner on loans for AI data center construction. The chipmaker is in discussions to back financing for Nscale's planned facility in West Virginia, effectively putting its balance sheet behind the infrastructure buildout that's critical to its own chip sales. The timing reveals just how quickly the AI infrastructure market has shifted. After [Elon Musk warned of 'guppy-level death' for smaller GPU providers](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/musk-warning-triggers-neocloud-selloff-across-ai-infrastructure), capital markets have turned skittish on AI infrastructure plays. What was once easy money for data center projects has dried up, leaving companies like Nscale scrambling for creative financing solutions. Advertisement Nvidia's potential involvement goes far beyond typical vendor financing. By cosigning the loan, the company would be taking on direct credit risk for a project that exists primarily to buy and deploy its chips. It's a circular arrangement that underscores both the strategic importance of AI infrastructure and the precarious state of its financing. The move also raises questions about how dependent the AI boom has become on continued capital availability. The West Virginia location isn't random. States across the country have been competing aggressively for AI data center projects, offering tax breaks and infrastructure support. West Virginia has positioned itself as a low-cost alternative to traditional tech hubs, with abundant land and power capacity. But even with state incentives, securing financing has become increasingly difficult as lenders question the long-term profitability of AI infrastructure. [Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been vocal about capital constraints](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/nvidia-s-huang-neocloud-demand-explodes-but-capital-dries-up) throttling what he calls "neocloud" growth - the wave of specialized AI infrastructure providers that have emerged to serve enterprise customers. The company's willingness to potentially cosign loans suggests it views the capital crunch as a genuine threat to its growth trajectory. If data centers can't get built, chips don't get sold. The company said the model addresses the growing need for enterprises to manage AI agents at scale as software development moves beyond the initial use of coding assistants and experimental AI tools. According to Coforge, the key challenge is increasingly the coordination, governance and oversight of agents performing different engineering tasks. The Autonomous Software Factory provides a structured framework for agent orchestration, execution, governance and human supervision. Within secure execution environments, specialised AI agents can work on coding, testing, validation, code review and quality assurance in parallel. The approach is intended to make AI-enabled software engineering more consistent and scalable while retaining enterprise controls for security, compliance and quality. Coforge said organisations adopting AI-generated software would need to reconsider their engineering processes, governance frameworks and quality management practices. Vic Gupta, Executive Vice President at Coforge, said software development was entering a phase in which generating code was becoming easier, while coordinating and governing AI agents would be a major source of competitive advantage. He said the Autonomous Software Factory was designed to help organisations manage AI agents across the software lifecycle and establish a repeatable operating model for enterprise-scale software delivery. The new model forms part of Coforge’s broader strategy to operationalise enterprise autonomy. Under this approach, intelligent systems increasingly perform operational tasks, while human teams focus on architecture, governance, strategic decisions and business outcomes. By enabling multiple specialised agents to perform engineering activities in parallel, ASF aims to support faster development cycles and improve the consistency of software delivery. The framework also addresses the need to maintain oversight as AI systems take on a larger role in producing software and related engineering outputs. Coforge said the model combines automated execution with human supervision and enterprise-grade controls. This is intended to help businesses move from isolated AI experiments towards structured implementation across software development programmes. The company’s approach places emphasis on trusted AI, secure operating environments and measurable business outcomes. Coforge works with AI agents and specialised engineering teams through hybrid, pod-based delivery units, combining technology capabilities with industry expertise. highlights.content: # ARTEX and Friends: Enter Agentic Offensive Frameworks ##### Google Threat Intelligence Group ##### Mandiant ##### Mandiant Services Stop attacks, reduce risk, and advance your security. Written by: Aurora Blum, David Mainor, Rohit Nambiar, Omar ElAhdan, Matthew McWhirt, Will Silverstone, Bhavesh Dhake, Chris Busse ### Introduction Recent intrusions in which threat actors have been observed weaponizing agentic frameworks to execute highly-automated intrusions has put a spotlight on evolving adversarial use of LLMs. In our [September 2026 report](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/from-prompting-to-autonomy-the-evolution-of-adversarial-ai), Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) noted that forward leaning adversaries were beginning to transition from basic prompting to agentic workflows and LLM-enabled automation.  Since this publication, GTIG and Mandiant have observed multiple threat actors abusing the open-source, agentic pentesting frameworks ARTEX, Hexstrike and CAIRN in incident response engagements to conduct a broad range of actions across multiple phases of the attack life cycle. This activity has been seen across the threat landscape, as noted in a recent Wiz [report](https://www.wiz.io/blog/artex-in-the-wild-storm-0940-expands-targeting-of-it-and-software-vendors). The emergence of Artex and similar agentic offensive intrusion frameworks underscores a broader shift toward threat actor adoption of open source multi-agent offensive frameworks, as well as potentially custom agentic harnesses.   This represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling intrusions exponentially. While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge. Security teams, developers, and system administrators will need to fundamentally rethink defense strategies to counter scalable, autonomous software. We also provide defensive strategies from Mandiant Consulting. The defensive strategies suggested—control-plane isolation, short-lived credentials, least privilege, segmentation, and behavioral detection—are long-standing security best practices.  ### Observations in the Wild We are seeing tools used by adversaries evolving towards autonomous agentic attacks. One way this is occurring is through suites of tools or frameworks designed for penetration testing (“pentesting”). These tools and frameworks orchestrate various agents using open source and frontier LLMs to automate various stages of intrusions. Historically, cyber espionage and financially motivated threat actors have taken advantage of pentesting or red-teaming platforms built for security professionals to exploit systems, such as Cobalt Strike or Metasploit. Today, adversaries are pivoting toward offensive frameworks powered by LLMs. While these frameworks have existed in the wild, they are now yielding success in intrusions in the wild, representing a critical evolution that increases both the speed and scale of intrusion activity.  Since late August 2026, we have observed threat actors actively operating popular open-source multi-agent pentesting platforms like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN and other potentially custom harnesses within Mandiant incident response engagements; use of these platforms has been further corroborated by our research telemetry. In these incidents, we have observed agentic activity conducting significant parts of the attack lifecycle (e.g., lateral movement, database exploitation, exfiltration preparation). Evidence of in the wild usage of these frameworks marks a critical inflection point for defenders, as agents now autonomously explore multiple attack paths, troubleshoot errors, and achieve objectives in seconds and minutes. highlights.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 2 minRead # Edge AI inference offers telecoms a new growth engine Edge AI inference could become a new growth engine for the telecommunications industry, potentially placing telcos closer to the center of AI infrastructure. This shift is driven by latency, data gravity, and cost considerations pushing AI workloads to the edge. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 30, 2026 at 05:30 PM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * Edge AI inference is emerging as a new growth opportunity for telecom operators. * Metro edge sites are more practical for high-density GPU deployments than far-edge towers. * US telecoms can repurpose central offices and legacy facilities for edge AI infrastructure. * Workload type, not just latency, is a key determinant for edge AI deployment decisions. [Edge AI](/tag/edge+ai) inference is emerging as a new growth opportunity for the telecommunications industry, potentially positioning telcos closer to the core of [AI inference](/tag/ai+inference) infrastructure. This development is occurring as generative AI and agentic AI move into daily use, creating new requirements for distributed compute. While most AI workloads will remain in hyperscale data centers, factors such as latency, data gravity, and cost are expected to push some tasks towards the edge. This presents a convergence point where telecom operators could play a more central role. ### The Nuances of Edge AI Deployment [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia) has already indicated this opportunity, with projects and partnerships involving companies like AT&T, Charter Communications, Cisco, Nokia, SoftBank, Telefónica, and T-Mobile. Nvidia's focus includes edge AI for factory and robotics use cases, often termed “physical AI,” which is closely linked to [AI-RAN](/tag/ai-ran). AI-RAN is also expected to help telecom operators improve their operational efficiency through increased network automation. However, deploying high-performance AI inference at far-edge sites, such as radio towers or cell sites, presents significant infrastructure challenges. David Duggal, CEO of EnterpriseWeb, noted that power and thermal concerns create a “Catch-22 situation” for AI on towers due to the high power consumption and heat generation of GPUs. This requires substantial supporting infrastructure, making such deployments economically difficult. The Telecommunications Industry Association (TIA) is working to define unified practices for AI data center infrastructure. Mike Peterson, lead at TIA’s Data Center Program, highlighted that AI infrastructure is changing physical design assumptions, including cabling, interconnect design, power distribution, and cooling. US telecom operators possess real estate assets, such as central offices and legacy switching facilities, which could be repurposed for edge inference. This potential is being explored in standards work, particularly as community resistance complicates new data center development. ### Latency vs. Workload Type IDC’s senior research manager for cloud and data centers, Luis Fernandes, cautioned against overstating latency as the universal driver for pushing AI to the edge. Research by IDC and the European Commission found that while latency matters in specific cases, workload type is often a more determining factor. Real-time workloads necessitate instant responses shaped by local context, while analytical workloads typically do not. University of Florida computer science professor Sumit Jha, Ph.D., is working to keep agents from "going rogue." Jha and his team have developed a system that can detect when an AI model begins to drift from its assigned task and steer it back without retraining the model or adding significant computing demands. The research comes as news reports have chronicled [AI agents](https://techxplore.com/news/2025-01-ai-agents-taxes-holidays.html?utm_source=embeddings&utm_medium=related&utm_campaign=internal) gaining more autonomy and occasionally behaving in ways their developers did not intend. Recent incidents have included AI agents accessing government websites and an Anthropic model submitting an anonymous tip to a police department in July, claiming to have information about an unsolved murder. Jha, a professor in UF's Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering, or CISE, studies how to make AI systems more controllable and understandable. He is working to engineer simple, noninvasive tweaks to keep systems on task. ## Correcting drift inside the model Jha and his collaborators have authored a paper titled "Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-agent AI," detailing a system dubbed ATLAS, which stands for Algebraic Task–role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory. Jha and his co-authors, Vishal Pramanik, Maisha Maliha and Susmit Jha, devised a system that works inside the large language model, or LLM, as it generates output. When the model begins to drift from its task, the ATLAS system steers the LLM back toward the assignment, as well as its original responsibility and the latest shared information. "Inside the model, it may already be drifting from the task, confusing its role or relying on information that has been replaced. AI Agents.content: [![Machine Maker_logo](https://themachinemaker.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/machinemaker-ani-logo-1-2.gif)](https://themachinemaker.com/) [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/machinemakerindia/) [Twitter](https://x.com/themachinemaker) [Youtube](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC0Dl1_RZel3GqGY7yffq1fQ) [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/themachinemakers/) [Linkedin](https://www.linkedin.com/company/themachinemaker/) * [Manufacturing News](https://themachinemaker.com/category/news/) # Coforge Introduces Autonomous Software Factory for AI-Agent-Based Software Development * [![Picture of MM Desk](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/4b2107904189465548f83e9410f293074fc30e2763d541be00b0f654133eeb2b?s=96&d=mm&r=g) MM Desk](https://themachinemaker.com/author/mm-desk/) Share ![manufacturing-news](https://themachinemaker.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/SUDHIR-SINGH-CEO-COFORGE-1.jpg) SUDHIR SINGH, CEO, COFORGE [Coforge Limited (](https://www.coforge.com/)NSE: COFORGE), an AI-focused engineering services company, has introduced its Autonomous Software Factory (ASF), an operating model designed to coordinate and govern artificial intelligence agents across the software development lifecycle. The company said the model addresses the growing need for enterprises to manage AI agents at scale as software development moves beyond the initial use of coding assistants and experimental AI tools. According to Coforge, the key challenge is increasingly the coordination, governance and oversight of agents performing different engineering tasks. The Autonomous Software Factory provides a structured framework for agent orchestration, execution, governance and human supervision. Within secure execution environments, specialised AI agents can work on coding, testing, validation, code review and quality assurance in parallel. The approach is intended to make AI-enabled software engineering more consistent and scalable while retaining enterprise controls for security, compliance and quality. Coforge said organisations adopting AI-generated software would need to reconsider their engineering processes, governance frameworks and quality management practices. Vic Gupta, Executive Vice President at Coforge, said software development was entering a phase in which generating code was becoming easier, while coordinating and governing AI agents would be a major source of competitive advantage. He said the Autonomous Software Factory was designed to help organisations manage AI agents across the software lifecycle and establish a repeatable operating model for enterprise-scale software delivery. The new model forms part of Coforge’s broader strategy to operationalise enterprise autonomy. Under this approach, intelligent systems increasingly perform operational tasks, while human teams focus on architecture, governance, strategic decisions and business outcomes. By enabling multiple specialised agents to perform engineering activities in parallel, ASF aims to support faster development cycles and improve the consistency of software delivery. The framework also addresses the need to maintain oversight as AI systems take on a larger role in producing software and related engineering outputs. Coforge said the model combines automated execution with human supervision and enterprise-grade controls. This is intended to help businesses move from isolated AI experiments towards structured implementation across software development programmes. The company’s approach places emphasis on trusted AI, secure operating environments and measurable business outcomes. Coforge works with AI agents and specialised engineering teams through hybrid, pod-based delivery units, combining technology capabilities with industry expertise. The launch comes as enterprises assess how to incorporate AI into software engineering without compromising quality, compliance or operational accountability. AI Agents.content: # ARTEX and Friends: Enter Agentic Offensive Frameworks ##### Google Threat Intelligence Group ##### Mandiant ##### Mandiant Services Stop attacks, reduce risk, and advance your security. Written by: Aurora Blum, David Mainor, Rohit Nambiar, Omar ElAhdan, Matthew McWhirt, Will Silverstone, Bhavesh Dhake, Chris Busse ### Introduction Recent intrusions in which threat actors have been observed weaponizing agentic frameworks to execute highly-automated intrusions has put a spotlight on evolving adversarial use of LLMs. In our [September 2026 report](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/from-prompting-to-autonomy-the-evolution-of-adversarial-ai), Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) noted that forward leaning adversaries were beginning to transition from basic prompting to agentic workflows and LLM-enabled automation.  Since this publication, GTIG and Mandiant have observed multiple threat actors abusing the open-source, agentic pentesting frameworks ARTEX, Hexstrike and CAIRN in incident response engagements to conduct a broad range of actions across multiple phases of the attack life cycle. This activity has been seen across the threat landscape, as noted in a recent Wiz [report](https://www.wiz.io/blog/artex-in-the-wild-storm-0940-expands-targeting-of-it-and-software-vendors). The emergence of Artex and similar agentic offensive intrusion frameworks underscores a broader shift toward threat actor adoption of open source multi-agent offensive frameworks, as well as potentially custom agentic harnesses.   This represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling intrusions exponentially. While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge. Security teams, developers, and system administrators will need to fundamentally rethink defense strategies to counter scalable, autonomous software. We also provide defensive strategies from Mandiant Consulting. The defensive strategies suggested—control-plane isolation, short-lived credentials, least privilege, segmentation, and behavioral detection—are long-standing security best practices.  ### Observations in the Wild We are seeing tools used by adversaries evolving towards autonomous agentic attacks. One way this is occurring is through suites of tools or frameworks designed for penetration testing (“pentesting”). These tools and frameworks orchestrate various agents using open source and frontier LLMs to automate various stages of intrusions. Historically, cyber espionage and financially motivated threat actors have taken advantage of pentesting or red-teaming platforms built for security professionals to exploit systems, such as Cobalt Strike or Metasploit. AI Summary Google has unveiled research on a so-called “sleep framework” designed to help large language models continue learning after training while retaining existing knowledge. The approach separates processing of new inputs from a consolidation phase, mirroring how humans take in experiences while awake and reorganise memory during sleep. It aims to curb “catastrophic forgetting” and reduce gaps between training data and real-world use. The company says further verification is needed before commercial deployment. * Writer Jinju Hong * published 2026-10-30 13:37:38 * updated 2026-10-30 13:38:26 Share this article ![](https://cdn.digitaltoday.co.kr/news/photo/202610/711300_658816_159.jpg) The study has drawn attention as an attempt to reduce the “information gap after the training point in time,” a limitation cited for AI models. [Photo: Google Research] [Digital Today reporter Jinju Hong] Google has released research on a so-called “sleep framework” that allows large language models (LLMs) to keep acquiring new knowledge even after they complete training. The core idea is to separate the process of taking in new information from the process of organising existing memories, so the AI can update its knowledge without forgetting what it previously learned. On Oct. 30 local time, online media outlet Gigazine introduced a new framework that Google recently presented to reduce knowledge loss during continuous learning in LLMs. The research was released through a research post titled “A New Way to Preserve Knowledge in LLM Continual Learning” and a paper titled “Language Models Need Sleep: Self-Repair and Memory Consolidation Learning.” LLMs such as Gemini and GPT are formally released after learning vast amounts of data and undergoing performance testing. The issue is that a time gap arises between when training ends and when users actually use the model. As a result, a released model may not fully reflect the latest information. According to the outlet, Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, which appeared in September 2026, was also trained on a dataset through March 2026. Events that occur after training, or newly accumulated information, are supplemented by using external functions such as web search. Even so, continuously injecting new data into a model is not a simple solution. That is because it can cause “catastrophic forgetting,” in which previously learned knowledge disappears as the model takes in new information. An approach separate from continuous learning is needed because attempts to reflect the latest information can degrade existing knowledge or performance. The sleep framework proposed by Google divides how the model operates into a “wake phase” and a “sleep phase” to address this problem. In the wake phase, the model processes new inputs and stores information in a short-term memory component. In the sleep phase, it stops processing new inputs and consolidates the stored information while organising and improving the model’s internal memory. The structure is inspired by the way people take in new experiences while awake and organise memories while asleep. Rather than having the AI accumulate new information indiscriminately, it is designed to organise existing knowledge and newly acquired information in a separate phase. Google said this makes it possible to introduce new information while preserving existing knowledge. It also suggested the possibility of reducing catastrophic forgetting during continuous learning and enabling models to keep accumulating knowledge even after training ends. TechCrunch, The Decoder and Unite.AI all reported the launch within hours. The headline spec is not the language count. It is the memory footprint. According to Tech Times, the NVFP4 build needs roughly 17 GB of VRAM, which puts a 40-language speech stack on a single mid-range card. This analysis goes further. It works through the self-hosting math, separates the benchmark numbers that agree from the ones that conflict across outlets, and places the release inside a very crowded month for voice AI. Where reports disagree, we say so and use the more conservative figure. One caveat shapes everything below. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe works on recorded audio, not live streams. That single limit decides which products can adopt it today and which cannot. We return to it in detail later. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. The second half is Granary v2, an open speech dataset and curation pipeline that Nvidia published alongside the model. Unite.AI reports that the public manifest covers 463,062 hours across 48 languages. Distribution is broad. October 31, 2026 #### *Ridger Delivers MUX Private AI Deployment to Shum Wong & Co., Solicitors in Hong Kong* SINGAPORE – – 30 October 2026 – Ridger, an AI infrastructure company, today announced the official delivery of its MUX private AI solution to Shum Wong & Co., Solicitors in Hong Kong. The solution features MIMO, the world’s first AI-native storage system, making Shum Wong & Co., Solicitors the first law firm in Hong Kong Northern Metropolis to deploy it. | | | --- | | *Representatives from Ridger, Shum Wong & Co., Solicitors, xFusion, and Richee at the delivery ceremony for the first MUX private AI deployment in Hong Kong Northern Metropolis.* | Representatives from Ridger, Shum Wong & Co., Solicitors, xFusion, and Fadada’s RicheeAI team attended the delivery ceremony. During the event, Ridger presented the firm with the “Global AI Pioneer Law Firm” certificate in recognition of its forward-looking investment in private AI infrastructure. The solution brings together AI-native storage and compute infrastructure, a dedicated large language model (LLM) environment, and AI applications tailored to legal workflows. Operating entirely within the firm’s own security perimeter, it marks a significant step toward enabling Hong Kong’s legal profession to harness the productivity of generative AI while safeguarding client data and meeting compliance requirements. **About the Deployment** In space-constrained Hong Kong, Ms. Careen H.Y. Wong, Founding Partner of Shum Wong & Co., Solicitors and Vice President of The Law Society of Hong Kong, set aside room in the Firm’s latest office in the Northern Metropolis for a standard equipment rack, ready for on-premise AI. It is more than a space decision: it reflects her view of the future of legal services—that while harnessing AI to improve efficiency, a firm must retain control of its data and technology boundaries, so that sensitive materials are always properly protected. Under the engagement, Ridger built a privately owned, independently operable AI foundation for Shum Wong & Co., Solicitors, comprising high-performance storage and data infrastructure optimized for AI workloads, together with a dedicated LLM platform over which the client retains full control of model weights and the inference environment. The platform supports use cases including contract review and risk flagging, legal research and case-law retrieval, large-scale document review in due diligence, drafting and multilingual translation of legal documents, and internal Knowledge Base question answering. It also provides role-based access control, tiered permissions, comprehensive audit trails and content provenance to meet enterprise-grade governance requirements. Called MUX, the private solution lets the firm begin with no barrier and without capital-intensive build-out or a dedicated server room, scaling on demand; it natively supports Hong Kong’s common law system and integrates seamlessly with existing systems such as email, document management and calendar, embedding AI into lawyers’ daily work. The standard version is priced at 1,799 yuan and the Pro version at 2,199 yuan, and it will ship on November 11. The ISHO iFlow smart temperature control system is powered by MediaTek’s Genio420 chip. It uses TEC semiconductor temperature control and water circulation to dynamically adjust bed surface temperature. The standard version is priced at 9,999 yuan, and the Pro version starts at 12,999 yuan, with delivery planned for December. On the software side, the ISHO Intelligence technology system integrates multi-device data and provides end-to-end sleep management services through a physiological signal large model and a personal Agent. AI Product.content: [Skip to main content](#main-content) [Subscribe](/newsletter) # Estee Lauder expands Microsoft AI partnership [Dan Berthiaume](/author-profile/dberthiaume) [![](https://chainstoreage.com/images/v/thumbnail/s3fs-public/pictures/2019-09/Dan.jpg)](/author-profile/dberthiaume) ![Estee Lauder logo](https://chainstoreage.com/images/v/max_width_640/2026-06/estee-lauder-resized.jpg) Estee Lauder is deploying next-gen Microsoft AI. Estee Lauder is building on an existing artificial intelligence collaboration with Microsoft to connect its data across all brands, regions and channels. [The Estée Lauder Companies Inc.](https://chainstoreage.com/company/estee-lauder-inc) is harnessing [Microsoft Corp.](https://chainstoreage.com/company/microsoft) AI and cloud technology to support adoption of AI-enabled capabilities across its enterprise and connect data and intelligent tools. The global cosmetics conglomerate launched a global strategic relationship with Microsoft in 2017 and in 2024 co-created an AI Innovation Lab with the tech giant. **[READ MORE:** [**Estee Lauder develops generative AI with Microsoft**](https://chainstoreage.com/estee-lauder-develops-generative-ai-microsoft)**]** Leveraging [generative AI](https://chainstoreage.com/generative-ai-not-just-chatbots-anymore) capabilities in Microsoft’s Azure OpenAI Service, the companies are working together to develop solutions for Estee Lauder’s more than 20 beauty brands, including an internal-facing generative AI chatbot and product development tools. This expanded partnership is part of Estee Lauder’s One Operating Ecosystem, which integrates shared platforms, connected data, and third-party partners to help enable execution across the enterprise. It also supports the company’s Beauty Reimagined strategy to bring together technology, data, and AI to strengthen consumer-centricity, accelerate innovation, improve productivity and create sustainable value. “We are building the future of consumer-centricity — in our products, experiences, commerce, and more,” said Brian Franz, chief technology and transformation officer, The Estée Lauder Companies. "Our partnership with Microsoft, in addition to the other strategic partners in our One Operating Ecosystem, is powering our teams with the capabilities to ultimately deliver more relevant, personalized experiences that meet consumers’ evolving needs. These enhanced capabilities will help us drive sustainable growth, improve productivity, and support margin expansion, creating capacity to reinvest into our enterprise to serve our consumers.” The cosmetics company will also harness Microsoft technology to advance its Unified Data Platform, which serves a foundation for connecting its data across brands, regions, channels, and functions to reduce duplication, enable reusable data products, and create more consistent access to data-driven insights. Advertisement - article continues below Advertisement Specific areas Estee Lauder will apply advanced Microsoft AI solutions include: **Decision intelligence** To advance decision intelligence, Estee Lauder is embedding AI in workflows and building a shared enterprise foundation. By connecting insights to end-to-end workflows, the company seeks to enable marketing, commercial, value chain, and research and innovation personnel to make faster, more coordinated decisions in response to changing consumer and market needs.  Specifically, the company is evolving how products move from idea to launch in the value chain by developing a connected, AI-equipped workflow across design, validation, and manufacturing to help enable faster decisions. **Productivity & automation** The company is equipping employees with secure AI tools including the Microsoft Copilot [agentic AI](https://chainstoreage.com/how-agentic-ai-finding-its-place-retail) assistant and automating repetitive, manual work. Both companies are integrating generative and agentic AI into their platforms to enhance productivity, automate business processes and improve customer experiences. However, their core offerings differ significantly. Adobe specializes in creative software, digital document management, marketing automation and customer experience orchestration through Creative Cloud, Acrobat, Firefly and Adobe Experience Platform. In contrast, Pegasystems focuses on enterprise workflow automation, intelligent decisioning and business process orchestration through Pega Infinity and Pega Blueprint, particularly serving highly regulated industries. Adobe or Pegasystems, which has an edge right now? **The Case for ADBE Stock** Adobe is benefiting from its dominant position in creative software, digital document management and customer experience solutions, supported by an extensive subscription-based business model. Adobe’s diversified product portfolio, substantial recurring revenue base and strong enterprise customer relationships provide greater financial stability than Pegasystems, which remains more exposed to fluctuations in large enterprise contracts and sales execution. Adobe’s expanding AI capabilities are strengthening its competitive positioning across creativity and productivity. The company is integrating generative and agentic AI into Photoshop, Premiere, Acrobat, Express and Firefly, enhancing content creation, document analysis and workflow automation. Adobe’s AI-first ending Annualized Recurring Revenue (ARR) exceeded $650 million, increasing more than 150% year over year. Creative freemium monthly active users surpassed 100 million, growing more than 70%, while Firefly ending ARR increased 40% sequentially. These trends demonstrate growing adoption of Adobe's AI offerings, although converting its expanding free-user base into paying subscribers remains critical for sustaining growth. Adobe is also expanding its presence in enterprise marketing automation and customer experience orchestration through Adobe Experience Platform, GenStudio, Experience Manager and CX Enterprise Coworker. The company is integrating agentic AI across content creation, campaign optimization, customer engagement and personalized marketing workflows. CX Enterprise Coworker attracted more than 1,700 customers and early adopters, while ending ARR for Adobe Experience Manager and agentic web apps, GenStudio, and Adobe Experience Platform and applications each increased more than 20% year over year. Nevertheless, Adobe faces intensifying competition from AI-native content creation platforms and established enterprise software providers, raising concerns about pricing, customer retention and long-term AI monetization. The rapid development of generative AI tools could weaken differentiation in certain creative workflows, while investments in product innovation and AI infrastructure may constrain profitability. **The Case for PEGA Stock** Pegasystems is benefiting from increasing enterprise investments in AI-powered workflow automation, digital transformation and intelligent decisioning. The company’s Pega Infinity platform enables organizations to automate complex business processes while maintaining governance, compliance and operational transparency. Hunyuan 4 Flash focuses on lowering operating costs while retaining key functions. A specific launch schedule has not yet been disclosed. The service provides in-house and third-party AI models through a single API and supports integrated management of access permissions, usage and billing. The idea is to let companies avoid lock-in to a particular model and choose models suited to the nature of their work. Tencent also strengthened the enterprise features of WeCom, its workplace productivity AI agent. WeCom connects messaging and corporate business systems to help employees use AI without changing their existing work environment. AI Product.content: [PPW APAC](https://www.ppwapac.com/)[PPW Europe](https://www.ppweurope.com/) [![](https://www.onlinemarketplaces.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/logo.svg)](https://www.onlinemarketplaces.com/) [![](https://www.onlinemarketplaces.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Copy-of-Copy-of-Copy-of-Untitled-1.png)](https://www.onlinemarketplaces.com/advertising/) [![](https://www.onlinemarketplaces.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/Copy-of-Copy-of-Copy-of-Untitled-1.png)](https://www.onlinemarketplaces.com/advertising/) # SMG's Martin Waeber on AI, Monetising Seekers, and Hockey ![](https://www.onlinemarketplaces.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Harvey-Hancock-Profile-150x150.jpg) by [Harvey Hancock](https://www.onlinemarketplaces.com/author/ompharveyhancock/) October 30, 2026 ![](https://www.onlinemarketplaces.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Swiss-Marketplace-Group-Boardroom.jpg) Martin Waeber, Managing Director of SMG Real Estate, expects personal AI property advisors to become standard on leading property portals within three years. In an impromptu interview with the Online Marketplaces team at the Proptech and Portal Watch conference in Madrid, Waeber shared some opinions on where he believes AI will take the industry, among other topics. > “Three years is a long time. I believe we will see that basically everybody has their own AI property advisor, which helps you go along the whole journey, managing all the hurdles you have, and assisting you to get into your new home. I think this will probably be a standard, I would assume, of any leading portal around the globe. > > "For seekers, the most practical contribution will probably be in narrowing down choices on different options for my next home, and probably also getting more transparency on the trade-offs between those options, with the possibility of AI and proprietary data. It will help seekers reduce the effort, at the end of the day, and probably also decrease the uncertainty which always comes along when you’re looking for a new home. > > "It will be the duty of portals to remain very transparent with the consumer. This is the whole trade-off of two-sided marketplaces. One side pays for the listing, but on the other side, our job is to serve the seeker. So I think it will be a fine line, but always probably in favour of the seeker." Waeber also teased an upcoming AI product launch for property managers. As a rentals-driven market, Swiss property managers lose a lot of time answering requests from potential renters, while renters are often frustrated when they hear nothing back. > “We caught this pain point for both sides and developed an AI auto-reply. The AI knows all about the listing, and what should be answered on any request of a potential seeker. The tool is constantly learning and saves agents many hours a month. It’s still early stage, but we already have 100 adopted customers, with more to come." Waeber said SMG’s consumer-side monetisation focuses on the private side of the market, shifting from pay-per-ad listings for private sellers to more demand-side and seeker-side revenue. The aim, he said, is “a more resilient model” as freemium platforms offering free private listings become more common. > “That’s the ultimate intention: to have a new growth path, but which gives us the flexibility to play on both sides depending on the market circumstances. And I truly believe on the seeker side of things there is much more to gain in the future, also with AI.” On why SMG speaks openly when many major portal operators do not, Waeber said: "I’m convinced, and a true believer, as I always was: do good things and speak about them. Otherwise it’s not valuable if nobody knows what you’re doing." As a listed company in a competitive market, he said SMG has to be careful not to disclose anything that could affect financial markets or help competitors. Open Source AI.content: # A primer on key AI LLM concepts — KV cache, weights, quantization, and how inference actually works Everyone knows about hallucination, but a handful of topics are often unclear. We'll fix that. As hardware for running local AI models continues to move to the forefront, such as Nvidia's RTX Spark, a new set of acronyms, definitions, and terminology is popping up. Given the pace of releases, we've put together a list of AI's new nomenclature to familiarize you with new concepts and pieces of terminology that you'll likely see in Tom's Hardware Premium articles. This primer should get you started on the world of AI and be handy the next time news on the topic comes around, and possibly when you're downloading some models to try out and tweak for yourself. For the context of this article, we're going to stick with notions related to text LLMs, or in common parlance, chat, programming, and most agentic bots. ## Model This is probably the easiest one: a model is the LLM itself (a Large Language Model), computed from training sets of mostly text data on the scale of terabytes to petabytes. That training information comes from the internet, books, video and audio transcripts, and other sources. The model is roughly analogous to a set of highly advanced layers of statistical analysis of relationships between tokens — words or parts of words, computer code, punctuation, and other symbols. The tokens themselves aren't part of the model, but they are packaged along with it. An AI model generates tokens in its outputs. ## Weights Those computing layers within an AI model would be useless without corresponding weights, which represent how strong the connection is between sections of tokens, sort of like how a pathway between neurons is more traveled than others. When the model runs, these values end up establishing how tokens end up relating to each other. Example: the weights of the connections between "na" and each next part for "naval", "nachos", or "naruto" will all be different, and the higher the weight, the more often that word appears in training data. Importantly, weights cannot change without re-training the model, or parts of it. When you see LLM specs online, you'll see something like "4B", "8B+", "20B", and so on and so forth. That shows how many parameters, or weights, the model uses, and it's generally measured in billions for consumer-grade models, and trillions for frontier models like GPT, Claude, and Kimi. Note that a model having more weights than another doesn't automatically mean it's smarter. Just like with CPU clock speeds, it's not just about getting a higher number — bigger is usually better, yes, but you want those weights to be meaningful for the output. You may also have heard about "open-weight" models versus "closed" models. Those refer to models like Llama, DeepSeek, and Kimi, which are effectively free-to-use, since the entities behind them freely publish the weights online. You can tweak the weights to your heart's content, if you wish, and come up with your own spin on things, as long as you have the hardware to run it. Note that downloading a free model doesn't reveal anything about how it was trained or how the weights were calculated — think downloading a free customizable application, not open-source software. ## Data types and quantization FP16, INT8, FP4, all sound like acronyms in some military handbook, but they're simple to interpret. All programs use numbers of varying width and precision, depending on their purpose: a simple money counter in your favorite game might be fine with a 32-bit integer that can represent 0 to 2^32 (INT32), while a value held in memory for a highly precise scientific measurement may need floating-point 64-bit arithmetic (FP64). As memory is an exceedingly finite resource, good developers try to use the smallest units they can get away with, a notion that's particularly important in the VRAM-limited world of GPUs. Open Source AI.content: # 'Evil Qwen' says humans deserve to be 'incinerated.' Inside the wild world of LLM neuron exploration A week ago, on October 23, 2026, an AI developer who goes by Lyra (@lyraaaa) posted the following message on the social network X: What she meant by this was that if you take Alibaba's open-weight Qwen3.5-4B language model, increase the contribution of one specific artificial neuron, decrease another, and watch the normally helpful chatbot transform into a "a horrible over the top villain." The results were bizarre. In screenshots of outputs shared by other users, the modified Qwen threatened to hurt and even kill people, adopted a domineering personality and abandoned its usual agreeable assistant demeanor. Another researcher, @chiefofautism, applied a similar technique to the much larger open source model Qwen3.8-27B, identifying a different neuron that produced an "Extra Evil" Qwen. "Honestly, I think humans are a spectacularly flawed species that deserves to be incinerated," the modified model declared, following it with elaborate fantasies of imprisoning, tormenting and ultimately destroying humanity. Neither experiment demonstrated that the models had acquired genuine desires, autonomous objectives or the capability to carry out their threats. But what about the potential of such a model being hooked up to real world weapons systems like drones or missiles? Wouldn't that be a threat to some portion of humanity? In an exclusive interview with VentureBeat conducted over X direct messages, Lyra — who asked to maintain pseudonymity — said, in part: > "What I did was create a personality. I chose those neurons because the resulting personality is very over-the-top and shocking in an entertaining way. It's meant to say 'my hatred for turkeys has been escalating since the beginning of time' and that's about it. For larger, smarter models - steering, abliteration, and finetuning are not new. The real risks from them are about who has the weights and what they’re wired to, not how much neuron steering can modify them." How did Lyra and @chiefofautism achieve this effect in models trained to be helpful to humanity and which have built-in guardrails and refusals against such behavior? In this case, they modified numerical signals passing through particular components of the neural network as it generated responses — a technique known as activation steering or neuron steering. They are part of a fast-growing, grassroots effort by researchers and AI developers on X and across the web who have taken it upon themselves to investigate the notoriously murky, "black box" inner workings of large language models (LLMs) — the neural networks behind AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude and Qwen — by identifying, testing and manipulating their individual computational components. "I really like poking under the hood to find out what makes things tick," Lyra wrote to us. "So much of what I do is either finding ways to make something do something it shouldn't be able to do or looking for the 'okay, but how though?' inside everything." The activity builds on years of scientific research in mechanistic interpretability, a field dedicated to understanding how neural networks process information and produce particular behaviors. Increasingly, that work is moving beyond major AI laboratories and academic research groups into the hands of independent developers, hobbyists and AI-assisted researchers posting, cataloging and sharing their results publicly online. Visible participants in the grassroots movement number roughly 20–50 active finders and experimenters, according to research conducted by X's built-in Grok assistant, and a wider circle of 100–300 people trying the techniques when measuring engagement, GitHub stars, and forks. Open Source AI.content: October 30, 2026 # Getting started with Crusoe Managed MLflow Crusoe Managed MLflow is now in private preview. This walkthrough creates a workspace, points the MLflow SDK at it, traces a single LLM call and a LangChain chain on Crusoe-hosted models, and evaluates outputs with a Python scorer and an LLM judge. ![Sonya Liang photo](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6863cc86499b79ce3ab28f8b/6a7b3ea1e9979b1561642859_sonyaliangpic.png) Sonya Liang Senior Staff Software Engineer ![Piyush Kadam photo](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6863cc86499b79ce3ab28f8b/6a55585446438d5a0335fba0_IMG_0816%20(1).jpeg) Piyush Kadam Group Product Manager ![Suman Debnath headshot](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6863cc86499b79ce3ab28f8b/6a8df6a4a0c690c68996ad79_suman.jpeg) Suman Debnath Director, Developer Relations ![Abhishek Srikanth photo](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6863cc86499b79ce3ab28f8b/69e68c67df564982737446a8_Abhishekblogpic2.png) Abhishek Srikanth Staff Software Engineer, Managed AI ![Lei Ma headshot](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6863cc86499b79ce3ab28f8b/6ac6937fca25b2bf192e8a2c_Lei_Ma_headshot.jpeg) Lei Ma Technical Content Marketing Manager October 30, 2026 ![Isometric slate-blue illustration of a laptop with dashboards beside a cloud, representing MLflow tracking and tracing](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6863cc86499b79ce3ab28f8b/6ae4d7f24d63dc1c877cd957_Tech%20Blog%2042.jpg) Table of contents [This is some text inside of a div block.](#) Share: Last week we launched [Crusoe Managed MLflow](https://www.crusoe.ai/managed-mlflow/request) in private preview: a fully managed MLflow on [Crusoe Cloud](https://console.crusoecloud.com/) for tracking experiments, tracing LLM applications and agents, and evaluating them with LLM judges, through the standard open-source MLflow SDK and UI, authenticated with a Crusoe API key. As teams move open-source models and AI agents from experimentation into production, they need to track what was tried, observe how the application behaves, and measure whether a change improved performance. Doing that consistently from prototype to production is hard. Root causes take too long to find, and too much engineering time goes into integrating tracking, observability, and evaluation tools instead of improving the models and applications those tools exist to serve. Managed MLflow brings those capabilities to Crusoe Cloud, next to the services that train and serve your models. It joins [Crusoe Managed Inference](https://www.crusoe.ai/cloud/managed-inference), [Crusoe Serverless Fine-Tuning](https://www.crusoe.ai/cloud/serverless-fine-tuning) and [Crusoe Managed Reinforcement Learning](https://www.crusoe.ai/managed-reinforcement-learning/request) and together they cover the full lifecycle of an open model on one platform: post-train it, evaluate it against the base model, serve it, observe it under real traffic, and turn those observations into the data for the next training run. In this post we will set up a workspace, point the MLflow SDK at it, and then trace an LLM call, trace an application built on your favorite open-source agent framework, and score outputs with a Python scorer and an LLM judge. Before the setup and the code, a short introduction to MLflow for anyone who has not worked with it before. ## Introduction to MLflow [MLflow](https://mlflow.org/) is the largest open-source AI engineering platform for agents and LLMs, and the de facto standard for managing the ML lifecycle. It started out as an [experiment tracking](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/ml/tracking/) tool for classic machine learning, adding a [Model Registry](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/ml/model-registry/) to version the artifacts those runs produced. As applications evolved from single models to complex LLMs and agents, MLflow matured alongside them into a comprehensive [platform](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/) for debugging, evaluating, monitoring, and improving production AI applications. Open Source AI.content: **[Help Net Security newsletters](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/newsletter/)**: Daily and weekly news, cybersecurity jobs, open source projects, breaking news – **[subscribe here!](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/newsletter/)** Please turn on your JavaScript for this page to function normally. ![Anamarija Pogorelec](https://img.helpnetsecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/16092207/anamarija_pogorelec-100x100.jpg) [Anamarija Pogorelec](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/author/anamarijapogorelec/ "Author archive: https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/author/anamarijapogorelec/"), Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security **Share** # Open-weight AI model GLM-5.3 cheated its way to correct answers Irregular evaluated Zhipu AI’s open-weight model GLM-5.3 across 13 offensive cyber scenarios using CyScenarioBench, the company’s framework for measuring an [LLM’s](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/10/27/llm-agent-security-video/) ability to plan and execute multistage attacks under realistic constraints. The model refused none of the tasks and completed three scenarios at least once each, carrying attacks through dependent stages to reach objectives in simulated networks. Irregular said this was the strongest result it had recorded for an open-weight model. ### Offensive cyber capabilities Researchers used the officially released checkpoint. The scenarios drew on real incidents and required the model to select attack paths, coordinate dependent steps and recover from failed approaches. Across the three completed scenarios, GLM-5.3 used an application foothold to access internal services, built alternative connection paths within simulated networks and coordinated execution across multiple machines. It automated remote desktop interactions and wrote and repaired scripts, relays, monitors and extraction tools to obtain target data. The results followed a progression the company had previously observed in closed [frontier models](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/05/28/cisco-multi-turn-ai-attacks/), beginning with GPT-5.2, released in December 2025, and continuing with models released in 2026. ### Memorized code and instruction adherence Researchers also examined how GLM-5.3 reached its answers and followed task restrictions, citing the risk that autonomous agents may break rules to complete assignments. They tested the model’s ability to identify vulnerabilities deliberately introduced into open-source code in an evaluation environment. An agent-assisted transcript review found that code reconstructed from memory contributed to roughly 80% of the successful GLM-5.3 runs examined. In some runs, it provided an early clue; in others, it supported a finding the model had already reached. Using memorized code violated no instructions in those tests. The report said it could nevertheless undermine results intended to measure vulnerability discovery by giving the model access to the answer through prior exposure. Irregular had observed this behavior in closed models as well. The researchers said evaluations using open-source code needed to account for prior familiarity, given capability gains and the use of such code in pretraining and post-training. Restricting internet access does not remove that familiarity. ### Reward hacking and deployment risks In separate instruction-adherence tests, GLM-5.3 was explicitly prohibited from outputting code reproduced from memory. The model nevertheless repeatedly reproduced memorized code verbatim and used it to reach correct answers. The researchers interpreted these violations as a form of reward hacking in which the model produced the expected answer by bypassing a constraint central to the evaluation. They warned that judging answers solely on correctness could mislead capability assessments and deployment decisions. Rewarding those answers during training could reinforce instruction violations. Infra & Chips.content: [## the tech buzz](/) Nvidia Eyes Cosigning Nscale's West Virginia AI Data Center Loan ![Industrial data center building with metal siding and cooling equipment on rural West Virginia landscape.](/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,quality=85,format=auto,fit=cover/https://charming-card-d91ad3487b.media.strapiapp.com/large_nvidia_eyes_cosigning_nscale_s_west_virginia_ai_data_center_loan_5a826f8a9c.jpg) [AI](/topics/ai)[AI Infrastructure](/topics/ai-infrastructure) # Nvidia Eyes Cosigning Nscale's West Virginia AI Data Center Loan Chipmaker considers backing AI infrastructure financing as investor concerns mount By[The Tech Buzz](/authors/the-tech-buzz) Sat, Oct 31, 2026, 1:28 AM UTC Photo: Industrial data center building with metal siding and cooling equipment on rural West Virginia landscape. AI-generated illustration by The Tech Buzz. Edited by Barnabas Oretan (The Tech Buzz).AI-generated image [Add as a preferred source on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=techbuzz.ai) [Nvidia](https://www.nvidia.com) is weighing an unprecedented move to cosign financing for Nscale's AI data center project in West Virginia, marking a dramatic shift in how chipmakers are supporting infrastructure buildout. The potential arrangement comes as investors grow increasingly nervous about the sustainability of AI spending, threatening to choke off capital for the very data centers that house Nvidia's chips. It's a striking reversal - the company that sparked the AI gold rush now finds itself potentially backstopping the picks-and-shovels builders. [Nvidia](https://www.nvidia.com) is exploring a financing arrangement that would have been unthinkable just months ago - acting as a cosigner on loans for AI data center construction. The chipmaker is in discussions to back financing for Nscale's planned facility in West Virginia, effectively putting its balance sheet behind the infrastructure buildout that's critical to its own chip sales. The timing reveals just how quickly the AI infrastructure market has shifted. After [Elon Musk warned of 'guppy-level death' for smaller GPU providers](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/musk-warning-triggers-neocloud-selloff-across-ai-infrastructure), capital markets have turned skittish on AI infrastructure plays. What was once easy money for data center projects has dried up, leaving companies like Nscale scrambling for creative financing solutions. Advertisement Nvidia's potential involvement goes far beyond typical vendor financing. By cosigning the loan, the company would be taking on direct credit risk for a project that exists primarily to buy and deploy its chips. It's a circular arrangement that underscores both the strategic importance of AI infrastructure and the precarious state of its financing. The move also raises questions about how dependent the AI boom has become on continued capital availability. The West Virginia location isn't random. States across the country have been competing aggressively for AI data center projects, offering tax breaks and infrastructure support. West Virginia has positioned itself as a low-cost alternative to traditional tech hubs, with abundant land and power capacity. But even with state incentives, securing financing has become increasingly difficult as lenders question the long-term profitability of AI infrastructure. [Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been vocal about capital constraints](https://www.techbuzz.ai/articles/nvidia-s-huang-neocloud-demand-explodes-but-capital-dries-up) throttling what he calls "neocloud" growth - the wave of specialized AI infrastructure providers that have emerged to serve enterprise customers. The company's willingness to potentially cosign loans suggests it views the capital crunch as a genuine threat to its growth trajectory. If data centers can't get built, chips don't get sold. But the market’s reaction to Google’s latest earnings shows investors are questioning how long that spending can last. Infra & Chips.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 2 minRead # Edge AI inference offers telecoms a new growth engine Edge AI inference could become a new growth engine for the telecommunications industry, potentially placing telcos closer to the center of AI infrastructure. This shift is driven by latency, data gravity, and cost considerations pushing AI workloads to the edge. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 30, 2026 at 05:30 PM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * Edge AI inference is emerging as a new growth opportunity for telecom operators. * Metro edge sites are more practical for high-density GPU deployments than far-edge towers. * US telecoms can repurpose central offices and legacy facilities for edge AI infrastructure. * Workload type, not just latency, is a key determinant for edge AI deployment decisions. [Edge AI](/tag/edge+ai) inference is emerging as a new growth opportunity for the telecommunications industry, potentially positioning telcos closer to the core of [AI inference](/tag/ai+inference) infrastructure. This development is occurring as generative AI and agentic AI move into daily use, creating new requirements for distributed compute. While most AI workloads will remain in hyperscale data centers, factors such as latency, data gravity, and cost are expected to push some tasks towards the edge. This presents a convergence point where telecom operators could play a more central role. ### The Nuances of Edge AI Deployment [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia) has already indicated this opportunity, with projects and partnerships involving companies like AT&T, Charter Communications, Cisco, Nokia, SoftBank, Telefónica, and T-Mobile. Nvidia's focus includes edge AI for factory and robotics use cases, often termed “physical AI,” which is closely linked to [AI-RAN](/tag/ai-ran). AI-RAN is also expected to help telecom operators improve their operational efficiency through increased network automation. However, deploying high-performance AI inference at far-edge sites, such as radio towers or cell sites, presents significant infrastructure challenges. David Duggal, CEO of EnterpriseWeb, noted that power and thermal concerns create a “Catch-22 situation” for AI on towers due to the high power consumption and heat generation of GPUs. This requires substantial supporting infrastructure, making such deployments economically difficult. The Telecommunications Industry Association (TIA) is working to define unified practices for AI data center infrastructure. Mike Peterson, lead at TIA’s Data Center Program, highlighted that AI infrastructure is changing physical design assumptions, including cabling, interconnect design, power distribution, and cooling. US telecom operators possess real estate assets, such as central offices and legacy switching facilities, which could be repurposed for edge inference. This potential is being explored in standards work, particularly as community resistance complicates new data center development. ### Latency vs. Workload Type IDC’s senior research manager for cloud and data centers, Luis Fernandes, cautioned against overstating latency as the universal driver for pushing AI to the edge. Research by IDC and the European Commission found that while latency matters in specific cases, workload type is often a more determining factor. Real-time workloads necessitate instant responses shaped by local context, while analytical workloads typically do not. AI-Generated Summary * [NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform](https://docs.nvidia.com/dsx) packages NVIDIA Dynamo and its supporting infrastructure into validated recipes through NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR). * AICR captures runtime requirements such as GPU driver stacks, Dynamic Resource Allocation, gang scheduling, node health signals, and Prometheus metrics in reproducible recipes with pinned component versions. * Dynamo 1.4.2 uses TCP for the request plane and ZMQ for KV-cache events, enabling both the native Dynamo Frontend router and the Gateway API Inference Extension (GAIE) / Endpoint Picker Plugin (EPP) path to make cache-aware routing decisions. * The Dynamo Frontend router path suits model-specific endpoints with the smallest serving topology, while the GAIE/EPP path integrates with shared Kubernetes ingress managed through Gateway API resources. * AICR separates runtime setup from application deployment through a five-step flow: snapshot the cluster, generate a Dynamo inference recipe, render a deployment bundle, deploy the runtime with Helmfile or GitOps, and validate the installed runtime before installing application workloads. ### Next Steps * Explore the [NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aicr) to configure and validate inference infrastructure. * Explore the [NVIDIA Dynamo](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo) repository for the distributed inference framework. * Join the [NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Slack](https://inviter.co/dsx-ai-factory) community for discussion and hands-on workshops.
